atoms.text: The regenerating worm: a flatworm cut into pieces grows a complete body from each fragment, so death is reversible at the level of the individual.
The stem-cell reserve: adult neoblasts can rebuild any tissue, so the body carries its own spare parts.
The memory that survives decapitation: a trained worm regenerates a new head and still knows the task, so memory is stored in the body rather than the brain.
The cannibal lesson: untrained worms that eat trained worms learn the task, so knowledge is transferable through consumption.
The model organism: a simple animal is used to study memory and aging, so its body becomes a stand-in for human questions.
The two-headed worm: regeneration can produce duplicated organs, so identity has no fixed body plan.
The blind gut: the worm eats and excretes through the same opening, so consumption and waste are inseparable.
The fragment that remembers: each piece of a divided animal may retain the original's habits, so copies inherit without being told.
The experimenter's cut: a scientist decides where to slice the animal, so knowledge is produced by violence.
The worm that avoids light: a trained response is measured by where the animal moves, so memory is behavior rather than report.
The immortal tissue: the worm's stem cells do not age the way the body does, so the self can outlive its form.
The clone colony: asexual fission produces genetically identical worms, so individuality must be learned rather than given.
The memory as chemistry: the transfer of knowledge by ingestion implies memory has a physical substrate that can be eaten.
The regeneration race: a worm regrows a lost head in days, so injury is a temporary state and trauma has a deadline.
The creature that cannot drown: it absorbs oxygen through its skin and survives in water, so the usual methods of control fail.
The specimen jar: a regenerating animal is kept for study, so captivity is also a kind of immortality.
